variants.title: Trace the sparse layer
variants.context: One multimodal sparse layer encodes media into tokens, fuses them into a shared sequence, scores and selects expert destinations per token, dispatches bounded assignments to expert devices, then weights the outputs and restores sequence order on the residual path.
variants.prompt: A text and image request reaches a sparse feed forward sublayer. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Group the assignments by destination device and exchange them within the expert capacity limit.
Tokenize the text and convert the image into model compatible token representations.
Produce expert scores for each token and select its top-k destinations.
Place both modalities in the shared sequence while preserving position and modality boundaries.
Weight the expert outputs, restore the original sequence order, and add the residual path.

variants.hint: The router acts on token representations, so something has to build them first.
variants.explanation: Sparse activation only saves compute when routing, capacity, and the dispatch and combine exchange all stay bounded and observable.

variants.title: Trace the sparse layer
variants.context: One multimodal sparse layer encodes media into tokens, fuses them into a shared sequence, scores and selects expert destinations per token, dispatches bounded assignments to expert devices, then weights the outputs and restores sequence order on the residual path.
variants.prompt: A high resolution image contributes far more tokens than its one line question. Put the stages in order, ending at the pressure point.

items.text: Fuse them into one sequence in which visual tokens dominate the count.
Enforce the per expert limit on a destination that is now far over its share.
Score every token and send most of the visual ones toward the same specialist.
Encode the short question and the large set of visual patches into tokens.

variants.hint: Which stage is the first to notice that one modality dominates?
variants.explanation: Token counts differ sharply by modality, so a globally healthy average can still hide one expert absorbing a visual burst.

variants.title: Trace the sparse layer
variants.context: One multimodal sparse layer encodes media into tokens, fuses them into a shared sequence, scores and selects expert destinations per token, dispatches bounded assignments to expert devices, then weights the outputs and restores sequence order on the residual path.
variants.prompt: Expert outputs are coming back from several devices for one sequence. Put the remaining stages in order.

items.text: Restore the tokens to their original sequence positions.
Multiply each output by the gate value that selection recorded for it.
Receive each expert's output for the assignments it accepted.
Add the residual path and continue into the later layers.

variants.hint: The gate values were produced earlier for exactly this purpose.
variants.explanation: Selection has to preserve gate values because combine is where they are spent, and order restoration is what makes the sparse layer transparent to the rest of the model.

variants.title: Enforce capacity honestly
variants.context: Capacity is enforced per expert over a routing group. The router scores each token, selection turns scores into bounded assignments with their gate values, capacity accepts assignments up to the limit, and an audit reconciles direct, rerouted, shared, and dropped assignments against the total.
variants.prompt: A routing group is processed at a sparse layer with a fixed capacity per expert. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Accept assignments up to each expert's limit and classify every overflowed assignment explicitly.
Turn the scores into bounded assignments and keep the gate values needed to combine outputs.
Verify that direct, fallback, queued, and dropped assignments reconcile to the total routed assignments.
Compute expert logits from each token representation and apply the routing rule.

variants.hint: The last step is an audit, not a transform.
variants.explanation: Conservation is the check that stops a cheap looking layer from hiding evidence it silently discarded.

variants.title: Enforce capacity honestly
variants.context: Capacity is enforced per expert over a routing group. The router scores each token, selection turns scores into bounded assignments with their gate values, capacity accepts assignments up to the limit, and an audit reconciles direct, rerouted, shared, and dropped assignments against the total.
variants.prompt: The vision expert overflows while the cross modal expert has spare room, under a second choice policy. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Reconcile direct, rerouted, and dropped assignments and record the load added to the fallback expert.
Fill the vision expert to its limit and hold the remaining assignments as overflow.
Score the tokens and select the vision expert for most visual assignments.
Send the overflow to the fallback destination that still has spare capacity.

variants.hint: The fallback destination gains work that its own budget did not plan for.
variants.explanation: A second choice policy preserves sparse processing only while spare capacity exists, and it changes expert semantics and load on the destination that absorbs it.

variants.title: Enforce capacity honestly
variants.context: Capacity is enforced per expert over a routing group. The router scores each token, selection turns scores into bounded assignments with their gate values, capacity accepts assignments up to the limit, and an audit reconciles direct, rerouted, shared, and dropped assignments against the total.
variants.prompt: One expert device fails mid batch. Put the steps in order, ending with what the report must show.

items.text: Apply the declared overflow policy to every assignment bound for that expert.
Report which modalities lost their sparse transform rather than reporting only a lower cost.
Route tokens normally, since the router scores do not know the device is gone.
Discover at dispatch that the destination cannot accept its assignments.

variants.hint: A cheaper layer is not automatically a healthier layer.
variants.explanation: Overflow is a model behavior, so the report has to name the evidence that lost its expert path instead of showing the saved compute alone.

variants.title: Do the capacity math
variants.context: Planning capacity per expert is the tokens in the routing group times top-k times the capacity factor, divided by the routed experts and rounded up. The formula counts assignments, not requests, and a shared expert is separate accounting rather than free compute.
variants.prompt: A routing group holds 960 tokens with top-2 routing across 12 routed experts and a capacity factor of 1.25. What is the planning capacity per expert?
variants.hint: Convert tokens into assignments before you divide.
variants.explanation: 960 tokens at top-2 make 1920 assignments, 1.25 headroom makes 2400, and dividing across 12 experts gives 200 assignments each.

mistakes.feedback: Left out the 1.25 capacity factor headroom.
Counted tokens instead of assignments, so top-2 routing was ignored.

variants.title: Do the capacity math
variants.context: Planning capacity per expert is the tokens in the routing group times top-k times the capacity factor, divided by the routed experts and rounded up. The formula counts assignments, not requests, and a shared expert is separate accounting rather than free compute.
variants.prompt: In one group the language expert receives 18 assignments, vision 52, layout 34, and cross modal 20, with a capacity of 28 per expert. How many assignments overflow?
variants.hint: An expert under its limit does not lend its spare room away by itself.
variants.explanation: Vision overflows by 24 and layout by 6, so 30 assignments overflow; the idle room on the other two experts is only usable if the policy reroutes.

mistakes.feedback: Subtracted total capacity from total assignments, which pretends idle room is automatically shared.
Counted only the busiest expert and missed the layout overflow.

variants.title: Do the capacity math
variants.context: Planning capacity per expert is the tokens in the routing group times top-k times the capacity factor, divided by the routed experts and rounded up. The formula counts assignments, not requests, and a shared expert is separate accounting rather than free compute.
variants.prompt: A group holds 720 text tokens and 1280 vision tokens. The layer uses shared plus top-1 routing, so every token also passes through the shared expert. How many expert assignments does the layer create in total?
variants.hint: How many expert paths does one token take here?
variants.explanation: Each of the 2000 tokens takes two paths, the shared expert and one routed expert, so the layer creates 4000 assignments; the shared path is real compute, not a free fallback.

mistakes.feedback: Counted the routed path only and treated the shared expert as free.
Counted both paths for the vision tokens only and left the text tokens out.

variants.title: Choose the control point
variants.context: Admission rejection, request queueing, and token overflow are different control points. Dropping an overflowed assignment skips the expert transform while the residual path continues, so it changes answer quality silently instead of returning an error.
variants.prompt: Traffic is well above what the deployment can serve within its latency target. Where should the system push back?
options: Lower per expert capacity so more assignments drop inside the layer.
Raise top-k so each token has a second expert to fall back on.
Reject or queue requests at admission, before inference starts.
optionFeedback: That trades a visible rejection for a silent quality change on served answers.
More destinations per token adds dispatch and expert work exactly when there is none to spare.
Correct: admission control protects the service target without changing model execution.
variants.hint: Which control point acts before any work has begun?
variants.explanation: Rejecting before inference protects the SLO, while skipping an internal expert assignment changes the answer after work has already started.

variants.title: Choose the control point
variants.context: Admission rejection, request queueing, and token overflow are different control points. Dropping an overflowed assignment skips the expert transform while the residual path continues, so it changes answer quality silently instead of returning an error.
variants.prompt: Average expert load looks even and the auxiliary routing loss is low, but document OCR answers have regressed. What should the team inspect first?
options: Assignment counts and gate mass broken down by modality and layer.
The aggregate auxiliary loss curve over the last training runs.
The total number of active parameters per token at serving time.
optionFeedback: Correct: a healthy global average can hide one modality receiving poor routes or losing its path.
A lower routing loss does not prove better multimodal answers.
Active parameter count describes cost, not which evidence reached which expert.
variants.hint: What does a global average hide when two modalities contribute unequal token counts?
variants.explanation: Routing evidence has to be sliced by modality, layer, and capacity state, because uniform token counts are not the same as useful routes.

variants.title: Choose the control point
variants.context: Admission rejection, request queueing, and token overflow are different control points. Dropping an overflowed assignment skips the expert transform while the residual path continues, so it changes answer quality silently instead of returning an error.
variants.prompt: Layout tokens, which carry the highest evidence weight for a document task, are the ones being dropped at overflow. The architecture has a shared expert with headroom. What is the best change?
options: Raise the capacity factor to four and keep the existing drop policy.
Send the overflow to the shared path and measure the added active compute.
Keep dropping, since the residual path still carries those tokens forward.
optionFeedback: Large headroom reserves memory and compute for every expert without fixing which tokens overflow.
Correct: a shared path gives a known general transform for the tokens that matter most, at a real compute cost.
The residual path is not the expert transform, and the highest weight evidence is exactly what should not lose it.
variants.hint: Not every dropped assignment costs the product the same amount.
variants.explanation: Overflow policy should be chosen from weighted evidence loss, because dropping a layout token and dropping a background patch are not equivalent.

variants.title: Keep the scopes separate
variants.context: Four scopes stay separate: tokenization decides how much evidence enters the sequence, routing decides which expert paths a token takes, capacity decides how many assignments an expert accepts, and serving places experts, batches work, and enforces latency policy.
variants.prompt: Match each scope to the decision it owns.

pairs.label: Tokenization scope
pairs.detail: How much text, image, audio, or video evidence enters the sequence at all.

pairs.label: Routing scope
pairs.detail: Which expert paths process each token at a particular sparse layer.

pairs.label: Capacity scope
pairs.detail: How many assignments a single expert may accept in one routing group.

pairs.label: Serving scope
pairs.detail: Where experts live, how requests batch, and how latency policy is enforced.

variants.hint: Two of these decide what happens to a token, and two decide what the system can afford.
variants.explanation: A request level model router that picks one whole model is a different mechanism from a token level router inside a model.

variants.prompt: Match each observed problem to the scope that owns the fix.

pairs.label: A single high resolution image floods the group with visual tokens
Most visual tokens pile onto one specialist while others idle
Assignments beyond the limit are silently skipped every batch
One device straggles and stretches the dispatch and combine time

variants.hint: Ask which decision would have to change to make the symptom impossible.
variants.explanation: Naming the scope prevents the common mistake of tuning the router to fix a problem created by tokenization or placement.

variants.prompt: Match each knob to the scope it belongs to.

pairs.label: Expert placement and batch size per destination

variants.hint: Each knob changes a different number in the same layer.
variants.explanation: The router, expert set, placement plan, capacity factor, and overflow policy are versioned together so a rollback restores one coherent contract.
